newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong-Beijing through train links two cities.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong-Beijing through train links two cities.

text.p: China and Hong Kong launched a direct rail service on Monday, linking the Beijing and territory just weeks before the British colony returns to Chinese rule.
The new service adds another exotic trip to the world's list of great train rides, a 29-hour, high-speed journey over 2,350 km (1,410 miles).
Both sides said the new, air-conditioned train service, launched in an era of increasingly popular air travel, would boost mutual relations.
Hong Kong's Financial Secretary Donald Tsang inaugurated the train service at the Hung Hom Railway Station on Hong Kong's Kowloon peninsula.

"It symbolises not only the close cooperation between the Kowloon-Canton Railway Corporation and the (Chinese) Ministry of Railways but also the strengthening of ties between Hong Kong and China, which so many people have been longing for," Tsang told hundreds of guests and passengers at the station.
Hong Kong, a British colony for 156 years, reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.
An official from China's Ministry of Railways echoed Tsang's view, saying it would promote ties between Hong Kong and the mainland.
"The rail link provides closer ties with our compatriots to ensure stability and prosperity," Zhang Zhengqing, chief executive of operation from the Ministry of Railways, said.
The first direct service between Hong Kong and Shanghai will also be launched on Tuesday.
The train services between Hong Kong and Beijing and Shanghai are a rare modern addition to the dwindling number of long-distance train rides.
The new link was welcomed by passangers in an era when more and more people -- including Chinese -- have opted for air travel instead of a romantic railway journey.

Tsang and Zhang, along with KCRC chairman Yeung Kai-yin and Transport Secretary Gordon Siu, sent the 448-seat train off from the station platform to the strains of a Royal Hong Kong Police marching band.

"We want to try the 'through train'. We are going to Beijing for sightseeing but mainly it's for the through train," said Kang Hyo Jung, a South Korean passenger travelling to Beijing with her husband.
"I think it's a historical moment," Kang told Reuters
Lam Jun-cheng, a Hong Kong businessman arriving on the first Beijing-Hong Kong train service on the same day, said the 29-hour ride was a good deal and a memorable journey.
"If it is urgent, I'll fly. If not, I prefer taking the train. The train is much cheaper," said the 60-year-old.

An adult ticket for a deluxe berth costs HK$1,191 (US$154), about three times China's average monthly wage, while tickets for the next class down, "soft sleepers", are HK$943 (US$120), and for "hard sleepers" are HK$706 (US$91).

While many passengers were euphoric about joining the inaugural journey, Lam complained that the customs check at Changping, in China's Guangdong province, before crossing the border into Hong Kong was inconvenient.
He said passengers had to drag their luggage out of the train for inspection and reload them on to the train afterwards.
